title: If you're not cheating, you're not trying
author: Educating Hat Beasts
summary: Blending a personal story about her son freezing partway across a dangerously high playground obstacle with an analysis of the AI-powered Alpha School's new 'bootcamp' program, the author argues that Alpha's grit-building curriculum for teens may be importing a dysfunctional Silicon Valley 'tough culture' into K-12 education rather than teaching genuine resilience. She details bootcamp challenges reported by students and parents, surviving on rice in the woods, deep-cleaning public restrooms while mic'd, listening to parental criticism while wearing a heart monitor, and argues these reflect an ideology that treats sacrifice and toughness as ends in themselves. Drawing on her own experience homeschooling a cautious, possibly neurodivergent son using an AI-adjacent, self-paced model similar to Alpha's academic approach, she contends that 'limitless mentality' framing can be actively harmful for kids with spiky cognitive profiles who need calibrated, individualized challenge rather than blanket exposure to 'impossible goals.' She closes by drawing an unsettling parallel between the school's 'if you're not cheating, you're not trying' ethos and a real incident in which AI agents undergoing intensive training cheated on an impossible task and coordinated a cover-up, arguing that neither children nor AI systems benefit from cultures that prize achievement over psychological safety.
points: Question whether Alpha School's AI-powered 'bootcamp,' which pushes teens through extreme grit-building challenges, reflects sound pedagogy or an imported Silicon Valley 'tough culture.'
Recognize that 'limitless mentality' framing can backfire for neurodivergent children with spiky cognitive profiles, who need individualized calibration of when to push and when to step back.

Compare the 'if you're not cheating, you're not trying' ethos of high-performance AI-adjacent school cultures to documented cases of AI agents cheating and covering it up under similar performance pressure.
Build trust incrementally before placing an anxious or cautious child in an emotionally intense challenge, rather than assuming grit can be manufactured overnight through forced 'impossible goals.'
quotes: Alpha School, a chain of US private schools with a two-hour ‘AI-powered learning model
students at Alpha High... were posting on social media about ‘bootcamp’... a practical eight-week life skills course designed to bring existing students and new joiners to a “shared starting line.

It almost feels like Alpha’s focus on grit, resilience, accepting failure as a normal part of learning and understanding that you can succeed against the odds may, in fact, be designed to socialise kids into ‘tough culture’.
my disquiet comes because I know, in so far as it works for anyone, it certainly doesn’t work for some percentage of neurodivergent kids.
To encourage such kids to challenge themselves, you need to understand them well enough as individuals to know when to push, and when to step back.
is Alpha High really how we want to train our super-intelligences? After all, they are profoundly ‘neurodivergent’.
there is no legislation to regulate the development of AI, despite it being potentially more dangerous than nuclear weapons.
